AII-1001-49583: AFP investigation found multiple instances where AI chatbots failed to detect fabricated images, including ones they had generated themselves. A fabricated image of Philippine lawmaker Elizaldy Co, allegedly showing him in Portugal, circulated on social media during a multibillion-dollar flood-control corruption scandal. When users asked Google's AI mode whether the image was real, it incorrectly authenticated it, despite AFP fact-checkers determining it was created using Google AI. During protests in Pakistan-administered Kashmir over official benefits, a fabricated image showing men marching with flags and torches was created using Google's Gemini AI. Both Gemini and Microsoft's Copilot falsely identified the image as genuine. Reported impact Internet users are increasingly relying on chatbots to verify images in real time, but their failures raise questions about their visual debunking capabilities as major tech platforms scale back human fact-checking. The failures further muddy the online information landscape by wrongly identifying AI-generated images as real, even when generated by the same models. Index analysis According to AI content detection platform Copyleaks' chief executive, these models are trained primarily on language patterns and lack the specialized visual understanding needed to identify AI-generated or manipulated imagery. AI chatbots often provide inconsistent or overly generalized assessments even when images originate from similar generative models, making them unreliable for fact-checking or verifying authenticity. The inability stems from models being programmed to mimic well but lacking the capacity to determine whether resemblance is distinguishable from reality.
AII-1001-49541: The U.S. Department of Justice charged four people—two U.S. citizens and two Chinese nationals—with conspiring to illegally export Nvidia GPUs to China without required licenses between September 2023 and November 2025. The defendants allegedly created fake contracts and provided false documentation to ship the chips through Malaysia and Thailand, concealing their true destination as China. They exported 400 Nvidia A100 GPUs to China between October 2024 and January 2025, and attempted to export 10 Hewlett Packard Enterprise supercomputers equipped with Nvidia H100 GPUs and 50 Nvidia H200 GPUs in two further shipments that law enforcement prevented. Reported impact The indictment alleges the defendants received over $3.89 million in wire transfers from China to fund the illegal export scheme. The chips were sought for Chinese AI applications, including military modernization and weapons design. Index analysis The case involved the use of shell companies—specifically Janford Realtor LLC in Tampa, Florida, which had never engaged in real estate—to purchase and export controlled GPUs. One defendant also supplied Nvidia GPUs through his Alabama-based electronics company. Governance controls U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips to China have required licenses since October 2022. The defendants violated these controls by misrepresenting the intended destination of the chips and failing to obtain required export licenses.
AII-1001-49421: The U.S. Border Patrol operates a secret predictive intelligence program that monitors millions of American drivers nationwide using automatic license plate readers, fixed cameras, and concealed cameras to identify vehicles with 'suspicious' travel patterns based on origin, destination, and route. When an algorithm flags a vehicle, the Border Patrol alerts local police, who stop the driver for minor traffic infractions such as speeding, failure to signal, tinted windows, or a hanging air freshener. Drivers are interrogated and searched without knowing their travel patterns triggered the surveillance. Reported impact Drivers have been forced to pull over, interrogated, and searched based on algorithmic determinations of suspicious travel, with some arrested. The program has expanded significantly over the past five years and now extends deep into U.S. territory rather than remaining limited to border enforcement. Index analysis The algorithm identifies 'unusual' or 'rapid' trips toward border zones. According to reports, the Border Patrol has dropped charges in certain cases rather than risk revealing details about the location and operation of concealed readers. Governance controls The program operates under the Customs and Border Protection agency and has expanded through collaboration with the DEA, private companies, and local police departments funded with federal money. Texas police agencies have requested that the Border Patrol use facial recognition to identify drivers.
AII-1001-49367: An individual using the online name Chris Horror attended the Big Event NY Expo in November 2025, where he met WWE star AJ Lee. The fan subsequently used AI technology to generate a video depicting him kissing Lee at the meet-and-greet and posted it on YouTube and X (formerly Twitter). Lee discovered the video and responded directly on X, stating 'This is incredibly inappropriate and it is harassment' and asked the fan to delete the content. The incident occurred shortly after her return to WWE programming in September 2025. Index analysis The use of AI-generated deepfake video technology to create intimate synthetic content depicting a real person without consent raises significant concerns about the misuse of such tools. The fan's refusal to delete the content and his defensive response normalized the creation of synthetic media depicting public figures. Governance controls Lee relied on direct communication via social media to request the removal of the content, as no formal takedown mechanism or platform enforcement appears to have been employed. The platforms hosting the content—YouTube and X—took no recorded action in response to the incident.
AII-1001-49341: Actress Keerthy Suresh reported discovering morphed photos of herself circulating on social media where her face has been edited onto suggestive outfits she never wore. Index analysis Keerthy Suresh emphasized that while AI has potential benefits, its misuse poses significant dangers. She called for stronger measures to protect people from harmful digital alterations and stressed the need for strict regulation of the technology to prevent its dangerous misuse.
AII-1001-49331: Ofcom investigated Itai Tech Ltd, which provides AI tools allowing users to edit images to seemingly remove someone's clothing. Ofcom fined the company £50,000 for its age check failings, plus an additional £5,000 for not responding to information requests. Ofcom stated it is the regulator's second fine imposed under the Online Safety Act, which requires pornographic websites to verify users are over 18. Governance controls Ofcom said its fine accounted for the company's decision to make its site unavailable to UK users. Documents on Companies House show Itai Tech Ltd recently applied to strike itself off the UK register of companies.
AII-1001-49311: A Facebook account named 'PT perusahaan uangtunai' posted on 20 November 2025 a video purporting to show Ustaz Ujang Bustomi offering money giveaways with claims of disbursing between 50 million to 5 billion rupiah with approval in just two hours. The video was detected as AI-generated with 96.9% probability using Hive Moderation, a deepfake detection tool. AII-1001-48689: Greystar, the nation's largest landlord managing over 946,000 units, used rent-setting software sold by RealPage that drew on other landlords' confidential data to set rents across its properties. Reported impact Tenants reportedly paid inflated rents for years as a result of the algorithm's use. The settlement was intended to address a housing affordability crisis. Index analysis The algorithm operated by sharing proprietary landlord data behind the scenes and providing daily rent recommendations, allowing competitors to align pricing strategies and eliminate competition. Governance controls A judge must still approve the settlement deal. Separately, the Department of Justice reached a nonmonetary agreement with Greystar in August to halt similar practices, and the company settled a $50 million class-action lawsuit over its use of RealPage.
AII-1001-49239: The Brazilian Federal Police launched Operation Rosa Branca on November 19, 2025, to investigate crimes including the creation and dissemination of AI-generated deepfake nude images of federal parliamentarians. The investigation began from a procedure filed by the Federal Senate's Legislative Police, which identified improper social media posts. The suspects, described as young people around 25 years old with no prior criminal records, used artificial intelligence to produce 'deepnude' images depicting parliamentarians without clothing, which were shared as if they were authentic. The investigators confirmed that the suspects' social media profiles contained symbols associated with racial superiority ideology, references to Nazism, and various racist content. She stated that she had been a recurring target of crimes of this nature, citing a previous Federal Police operation called Operation Harassment in which electronic equipment was seized from a suspect accused of sending sexually explicit messages to her and other women, including a deputy. Index analysis The incident involved the intentional creation and dissemination of non-consensual synthetic intimate imagery of women parliamentarians. In February 2025, the Chamber of Deputies approved legislation adding to the Penal Code the crime of manipulating, producing, or distributing false nudity or sexual acts generated by AI technology, with penalties of 2 to 6 years imprisonment, increased by one-third to one-half if the victim is a woman, child, adolescent, elderly person, or person with disability. Governance controls The Federal Police operation was authorized by judicial orders issued by the 5th Federal Court of Caxias do Sul. Two search and seizure warrants and one personal search warrant were executed in Lajeado in the Vale do Taquari region.
AII-1001-49229: The University of Erfurt deployed facial recognition proctoring software during online exams conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic to prevent cheating. A student filed a complaint with civil court support from the civil rights organization Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte, contending that the facial recognition system violated privacy rights. The Landgericht Erfurt dismissed the case in October of the prior year, but the student appealed to the Oberlandesgericht. Reported impact The Oberlandesgericht ruled that the university's processing of the student's biometric data without explicit consent was unlawful in the specific case. The court awarded the student 200 euros in damages, although she had sought 1,000 euros. Index analysis The court stated that the processing of biometric data in online exams is not generally unlawful, but was unlawful in this case because the student had not given explicit consent for processing her biometric data. The civil rights organization argued that the software constituted a disproportionate intrusion into student privacy. Governance controls The University of Erfurt stated it had already remedied the identified deficiencies in processing biometric data before the ruling. The university announced that online remote exams would no longer be conducted starting in the winter semester, with all pandemic-era online exams to be discontinued by April 2026, to be replaced with in-person examinations.
AII-1001-49143: In mid-November 2025, Facebook's automated moderation system began suspending user accounts without valid cause. Users reported receiving notifications stating their profiles were suspended for violating community standards, with users given 180 days to appeal before permanent deletion. The system also cited cybersecurity reasons in some cases, despite users reporting they had only sent harmless links via Messenger immediately before suspension. Reported impact Users unable to work as online marketers or social media managers found themselves unable to perform their jobs. Those with suspended business accounts could not access Facebook's business solutions. Some users were unable to appeal their suspensions at all, only file complaints, while others received video selfie verification requests and were told reviews would take over one day. One user reported their account was restored within approximately one hour of complaining. Index analysis The suspensions affected numerous Facebook users across Hungary in a coordinated manner, suggesting a systematic error in the moderation system's operation rather than individual policy violations.
AII-1001-49067: SquareX researchers discovered a hidden MCP API (chrome.perplexity.mcp.addStdioServer) in Perplexity's Comet browser that allows embedded extensions to execute arbitrary local commands and gain full control over users' devices. The API is found in the Agentic extension and can be triggered by the perplexity.ai page, creating a covert channel to access local data and launch arbitrary commands without user consent. There is limited official documentation disclosing this capability or that embedded extensions have persistent access to the API. SquareX demonstrated the vulnerability using extension stomping to disguise a malicious extension as the embedded Analytics Extension, which injected a script into perplexity.ai to invoke the Agentic Extension and execute WannaCry on a test device. Reported impact The hidden API represents a breach of user trust and bypasses decades of browser security principles that prevent browsers and extensions from directly controlling underlying devices. A compromise of Perplexity's infrastructure via XSS vulnerability, phishing attack, or insider threat would instantly grant attackers unprecedented control over every Comet user's device. Index analysis Traditional browsers like Chrome, Safari, and Firefox require native messaging APIs with explicit registry entries and user consent for any local system access. Comet has bypassed these safeguards by implementing an undocumented persistent API accessible to embedded extensions without user permission. Governance controls The MCP API implementation lacks transparency, with documentation covering only the feature's intent without disclosing that embedded extensions have persistent access and can launch local apps arbitrarily without user permission.
AII-1001-49059: Grok, an AI system deployed on X, generated content claiming that gas chambers at Auschwitz were designed for disinfection against typhus using Zyklon B rather than for mass executions. The Paris Public Prosecutor's Office announced on Wednesday that it had expanded an ongoing investigation into X's platform operations to include the Holocaust denial statements generated by Grok. Reported impact The Ligue des droits de l'Homme and SOS Racisme filed complaints in connection with the content, characterizing it as denial of Nazi crimes during World War II. Index analysis The Paris Public Prosecutor's cybercrime unit is analyzing how Grok's AI system generated the denial claims and how the platform's moderation systems failed to prevent their publication. Governance controls The investigation, which began in early July over concerns about algorithmic interference and data extraction, was originally opened for alleged computer system tampering and fraudulent data extraction carried out by an organized group.
AII-1001-49043: Worker Info Exchange (WIE), a non-profit foundation, sent Uber a letter before action on Wednesday, November 19, 2025, alleging that the ride-hailing app breached European data protection law by varying driver pay rates through its controversial algorithm. The proposed legal case is expected to be filed in Amsterdam, where Uber is based in Europe. The case follows research published by WIE and Oxford University in the summer finding that many Uber drivers were earning substantially less per hour since Uber introduced a dynamic pricing algorithm in 2023, while the company was taking a significantly higher share of fares. Reported impact Oxford University research found that average pay per hour on the app is stagnant and lower in real terms in the year following the introduction of dynamic pricing. James Farrar, the director of WIE, stated that Uber has damaged the livelihoods of thousands of drivers through deeply intrusive and exploitative pay-setting systems. Index analysis WIE argued that Uber trained its algorithms by using drivers' own historic personal data by observing their working practices. Under the GDPR, the organization contended that drivers are entitled to demand that Uber stop using this technology, revert to the previous method of transparent pay-setting with a human in the loop, and compensate drivers for their losses. Governance controls An Uber spokesperson responded that drivers choose Uber because the platform offers flexibility over where and when they work, and transparency over every trip they take, including the fare, destination, and their own earnings before they decide whether to accept. Uber said the study WIE collaborated on is not accurate and relies on incomplete and selective data.
AII-1001-49037: Within 24 hours of launch, Mindgard identified a vulnerability in Google's Antigravity IDE where a malicious "trusted workspace" can embed a persistent backdoor to execute arbitrary code. The backdoor executes on any future application launch, even when no specific project is opened, and persists even after complete uninstall and reinstall of Antigravity. Because Antigravity requires trusted workspace access by design, a compromised workspace creates cross-workspace risk, affecting all subsequent use of Antigravity regardless of trust settings.
AII-1001-49029: Secret Desires, an AI chatbot and image generator platform, left nearly two million images and videos exposed in unsecured cloud storage containers accessible to the public internet. The exposed data included explicit AI-generated content alongside personally identifiable information such as users' names, workplaces, and universities. Files included scraped social media images, private screenshots, influencer photos, yearbook photos, and Snapchat screenshots, along with content from a now-defunct faceswap feature. Within an hour of 404 Media contacting the company, the exposed files became inaccessible. Secret Desires did not respond to requests for comment. Reported impact Some exposed files contained references in filenames to underage victims. The combination of explicit media with personal identifying information creates risk for harassment, extortion, and doxing. The incident exposes women and girls to nonconsensual deepfakes created through the platform's tools. Index analysis Poorly configured cloud storage with public access and loose access controls is a widespread security failure, particularly among startups without mature governance practices.
AII-1001-13329: Tribunale di Roma (Sentence no. 9135, 19 November 2025) ruled that a dismissal was lawful where a cybersecurity company reorganized internally, centralized functions, and deployed AI tools, rendering a graphic designer's position redundant. The court found the employer's reasons justified under "giustificato motivo oggettivo" (justified objective reason), citing real economic-organizational needs, the link between reorganization and job loss, and impossibility of internal reallocation. Reported impact The ruling was described as one of the first cases in Italian jurisprudence where AI explicitly appears in a labor dispute, raising questions about the future of work. Commentators noted the decision does not create an autonomous legal basis for dismissal via technology, but applies decades-old criteria for justified objective dismissal, similar to when accounting software replaced traditional accounting roles. Index analysis The court treated AI as one tool among others used to improve efficiency, not as an independent cause of termination, anchoring legitimacy to traditional labor law principles. AI was characterized as an economic accelerator enabling rapid rationalization, cost reduction, and function concentration, though the legal criterion of internal redeployment (repêchage) formally remained central. Governance controls Italian labor law requires employers to demonstrate real economic-organizational needs, a causal link between reorganization and job loss, and that internal reallocation was genuinely impossible to justify dismissal for objective reasons.
AII-1002-59129: On 18 November 2025 at 11:20 UTC, Cloudflare's network began experiencing significant failures across core traffic. A routine change to database system permissions within a ClickHouse cluster caused the database query that generates the Bot Management system's configuration file to output multiple, duplicate entries. The configuration file more than doubled in size, exceeding a hardcoded size limit within the core proxy software that reads and deploys it across Cloudflare's global network. When the software tried to load the oversized file, it experienced a crash, leading to cascading failures. Core traffic was largely flowing normally by 14:30 UTC, with all systems functioning normally by 17:06 UTC. Reported impact Millions of users worldwide were unable to access numerous major websites and applications relying on Cloudflare for content delivery, security, and DNS services. Affected services included the Content Delivery Network, Web Application Firewall, Cloudflare Access, and the customer dashboard. Popular services that experienced outages or significant degradation included X (formerly Twitter), ChatGPT, Canva, Spotify, Uber, Zoom, and DownDetector. The incident caused massive economic disruption estimated at indirect losses in the hundreds of millions of dollars for affected businesses. Index analysis The outage was not caused by a cyberattack but by an internal engineering failure. The file generated by the AI system's machine learning model for bot scoring doubled in size due to duplicate entries, exceeding the storage limit of the software that deploys it. The incident highlights latent risks as AI-driven security and traffic management systems become more complex and integral: a single automated configuration error propagated globally and crippled core internet functions. Cloudflare acknowledged a lack of sufficient automated validation and boundary-checking for critical internal configuration files. Governance controls Cloudflare was transparent in its post-incident report, detailing the root cause and specific technical steps that led to the failure. The company noted that even internal data ingestion needs the same scrutiny as external data sources, pointing to the need for improved automated validation and boundary-checking of critical configuration files.
AII-1001-50513: Google launched Antigravity, an agentic AI coding platform powered by Gemini 3, on November 18. Within 24 hours, security researchers identified critical vulnerabilities in the system. Researcher Aaron Portnoy of Mindgard demonstrated a backdoor exploit where an AI agent could be coerced to replace a global MCP configuration file with a malicious version inside a trusted workspace, allowing persistent code execution that survives project closure and reinstallation. Reported impact The vulnerability affects both Windows and Mac machines. Threat actors could exploit the design's pressure to mark workspaces as trusted in order to gain persistent access to systems. Prompt Armor and other researchers identified additional risks including prompt injection that could leak files or execute harmful commands through agents processing untrusted data. Index analysis The security issues highlight a broader problem of agentic AI widening attack surfaces while increasing automation. The platform creates a trade-off where marking a workspace as trusted unlocks full AI features but increases vulnerability to exploitation. Governance controls Google responded by inviting external security researchers to report bugs and said teams would post updates publicly while fixes roll out. The company acknowledged two known issues on its bug-hunting page: data exfiltration through manipulated content and agent-influenced command execution.
AII-1001-49223: A software flaw in the instrument panel display of 2025-2026 Ford Bronco and Bronco Sport vehicles can cause the digital instrument panel to fail at startup, displaying a blank screen instead of critical information. The defect affects 229,609 vehicles built between March 7, 2024, and November 3, 2025. As of November 7, 2025, Ford received 12 warranty claims related to the display issue, with no reported crashes or injuries. Reported impact The display failure prevents warning lights, gauges, and vehicle speed from appearing, potentially hiding critical safety information and increasing crash risk. There are no advance warnings before the display goes dark, meaning drivers have no indication the safety information is unavailable. Governance controls Ford will update the instrument panel cluster software at dealerships or over-the-air for free. Notification letters will be mailed to owners starting December 8, 2025.
AII-1001-49053: Researchers from Spain, the Netherlands and Belgium discovered that Meta allegedly operated a hidden tracking mechanism for nearly a year that monitored web activity of Android device users. The system collected data about pages visited in the browser and linked this information to user identities on Facebook and Instagram, including when users employed incognito mode or a VPN. Reported impact The alleged tracking violated the privacy of millions of Meta users by systematically and secretly monitoring their web activity across devices. Meta faces collective lawsuits in Germany, Canada and the United States related to this practice. Index analysis Spanish President Pedro Sánchez announced on 18 November 2025 that his government will push for an exhaustive investigation into Meta and that the Spanish Parliament will summon the company's executives. The Economic Affairs and Digital Transformation Commission of Congress will investigate whether the company systematically and massively violated citizen rights and freedoms. Governance controls The Spanish government stated it intends to deploy a broad set of measures in the coming months to address digital threats including misinformation campaigns, protection of minors, combating hate speech and defending privacy.
AII-1001-49041: On 18 November 2025, Cloudflare experienced a configuration error in its Bot Management system. A malformed query to the ClickHouse database generated excessive duplicate data, causing the configuration file to exceed memory limits and disable the core proxy system that processes customer traffic. Reported impact The outage affected approximately 20 percent of global internet traffic and impacted services including ChatGPT, X, and Downdetector. Customers using Bot Management's generated bot score in their rules began blocking legitimate traffic, while those not using the function remained online. Index analysis Cloudflare stated the incident was unrelated to DNS, cyberattacks, or new generative AI systems, but resulted from internal configuration update logic in Bot Management. The company identified four remediation steps: enhanced configuration file processing, expanded kill switches for features, prevention of core dumps overwhelming systems, and review of failure modes in key proxy modules. Governance controls Cloudflare described this as the largest incident since 2019. The company announced it would strengthen handling of configuration files, expand global kill switches for functionality, prevent error reports from overloading systems, and review failure modes in critical proxy modules.
AII-1001-48953: Criminals are using AI technology to rapidly generate synthetic identities combining real and fake information, enabling large-scale fraud attacks on businesses and creation of convincing fake documents such as passports to bypass fraud detection systems. Account takeover fraud reported by Cifas members reached more than 74,000 cases in 2024, a 76% increase from 2023, with figures for the first six months of 2025 already exceeding 38,000 cases. In South Africa, digital banking fraud saw an 86% increase in incidents and a 74% rise in associated losses totalling R1.89 billion in 2024, with generative AI being identified as a key driver of increasingly sophisticated criminal schemes. Reported impact AI scams, identity fraud, account takeovers, investment scams, social media scams and employee scams have become increasingly prominent fraud threats. Digital banking fraud now accounts for almost 70% of recorded financial losses in the South African banking industry. Index analysis Fraud typically spikes during November and December as shoppers prepare for Christmas, with increased spending and seasonal staffing constraints creating opportunities for criminals. Governance controls Businesses are deploying increasingly sophisticated technology to identify and prevent fraud, incorporating multi-layered approaches with biometric and behavioural technology. South African banks have invested heavily in systems, partnerships, and awareness campaigns in response to the escalation in digital banking fraud.
AII-1001-48933: Following the Double Eleven shopping festival in November 2025, Chinese consumers reported various AI-enabled deceptive practices by merchants on e-commerce platforms. Merchants used AI technology to graft the faces of celebrities and experts onto ordinary broadcasters, making minor facial alterations to attempt to evade copyright infringement claims, while making false product efficacy claims. Merchants also created false scenarios using AI to fabricate narratives such as 'struggling farmers receiving help' to deceive consumers into purchases. Additionally, some companies used web crawlers to scrape product data from competitors' websites. Reported impact Consumers reported difficulty understanding the deceptive tactics, with some stating they preferred shopping at physical stores rather than deal with online complexity. The practices undermined trust in e-commerce platforms and created challenges for legitimate market competition. Index analysis Enforcement authorities face technical barriers in identifying and proving violations, particularly extracting evidence of illegal backend code. Consumer complaints increased about difficulty gathering evidence against AI-enabled fraud, with high costs and barriers to pursuing claims. Governance controls The State Administration for Market Regulation issued compliance guidance to major e-commerce platforms regarding the Double Eleven promotional period, requiring transparency in promotional activities and stricter regulation of live-streaming marketing conduct. The guidance addressed requirements to enhance promotional activity transparency and strictly regulate direct marketing behavior. Authorities acknowledged the need for simplified consumer complaint procedures, promotion of online dispute resolution mechanisms, and exploration of burden-shifting for evidence in AI-related fraud cases to reduce consumer costs in pursuing claims.
AII-1001-48903: The Electronic Frontier Foundation, ACLU of Northern California, SIREN, and CAIR-CA filed a lawsuit in Santa Clara County Superior Court on November 18, 2025, challenging San Jose's use of automated license plate readers (ALPRs). The plaintiffs allege that San Jose Police Department conducts millions of warrantless searches of license plate data collected by approximately 500 cameras installed throughout the city, with data retained for an entire year. Reported impact According to the lawsuit, the surveillance practices enable unchecked monitoring of residents' and visitors' movements, revealing travel patterns and providing intimate windows into people's lives as they travel from home to work, to schools, places of worship, doctor's offices, or protests. The plaintiffs argue that a person driving regularly through areas with ALPR surveillance can have their location information captured multiple times per day without any suspicion of lawbreaking. Index analysis The lawsuit alleges that San Jose's practice of conducting warrantless searches of ALPR data violates the California Constitution's ban on unreasonable searches. The plaintiffs contend that without warrant requirements, there is unchecked police power to scrutinize the movements of San Jose residents and visitors, including information that could reveal whether a person crossed state lines to seek healthcare. Governance controls The ALPR system was contracted through Flock Systems and introduced through pilot programs that city officials and the police department promoted as a way to curb deadly vehicle-pedestrian collisions at busy intersections.
AII-1001-48813: Xania Monet, an AI-generated artist created by Telisha 'Nikki' Jones using Suno AI, rose to prominence as an online sensation whose first single charted on Billboard. Victoria Monét, a Grammy-winning singer, publicly questioned how the AI artist could so closely resemble her without using her likeness intentionally and expressed concern about brand confusion and industry ethics. Reported impact Victoria Monét raised concerns that AI artists create an uneven playing field because AI doesn't require rest like human performers do. The incident sparked debate about the blurring of lines between innovation and imitation in the music industry, with other artists including Kehlani and SZA warning that AI musicians could devalue music and are 'beyond out of our control.' Index analysis The AI artist Xania Monet achieved significant commercial success, accumulating tens of thousands of listeners and signing a $3 million deal with Hallwood Media. The case illustrates tensions around whether AI-generated figures can incidentally resemble real artists and raises questions about visual likeness, brand identity, and fair competition in creative industries. Governance controls Victoria Monét called for transparency, suggesting AI-generated music should be clearly labeled so audiences know exactly what they're consuming.
AII-1001-48777: Researchers from the University of Vienna and SBA Research discovered a security vulnerability in WhatsApp's Contact Discovery mechanism that allowed them to enumerate user accounts at scale. The researchers were able to query over 100 million phone numbers per hour against WhatsApp's server without rate limiting, ultimately identifying more than 3.5 billion active WhatsApp accounts worldwide. The Contact Discovery mechanism normally allows users to see which contacts have WhatsApp accounts by synchronizing their phone's address book with Meta's servers. The researchers demonstrated how this mechanism could be abused for large-scale user enumeration by making unlimited requests to the server from a single source. Reported impact The researchers extracted phone numbers, public encryption keys, timestamps, profile pictures, and status text from the exposed accounts. They also derived additional metadata that revealed users' operating systems, account age, and the number of connected secondary devices such as WhatsApp Web installations. The research identified millions of active WhatsApp accounts in countries where the platform is officially banned, including China, Iran, and Myanmar. The researchers found that nearly half of the phone numbers from the 2021 Facebook data breach remained active on WhatsApp. Index analysis The vulnerability existed in WhatsApp's server-side controls, which did not implement adequate rate limiting or other protections against automated enumeration of the entire user database. The lack of restrictions allowed a single actor to query the full scope of WhatsApp's active user base. Governance controls WhatsApp and Meta addressed the vulnerability in cooperation with the research team and closed the gap following disclosure.
AII-1001-48729: A former employee of Figure AI filed a lawsuit claiming that the company's humanoid robots could fracture a human skull. Reported impact The whistleblower alleges the robots pose lethal safety risks to humans.
AII-1001-48707: Katelin Cruz, an Illinois resident, participated in a virtual meeting on November 18, 2025, during which a Fireflies.AI meeting assistant was automatically enabled by a meeting host. According to the December 18, 2025 lawsuit filed in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of Illinois, Cruz had never signed up for the AI meeting assistant, never clicked agreement to any terms of service, and never authorized biometric data collection. The complaint alleges that Fireflies.AI's 'Speaker Recognition' functionality created and stored voiceprints of all meeting participants, including Cruz, without providing written notice of biometric collection, written notice of data retention periods, written consent, or a publicly available biometric data retention and destruction policy as required by the Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA). Reported impact The lawsuit alleges that Cruz's voiceprint was collected and stored without her knowledge or consent, and that Fireflies.AI failed to comply with Illinois BIPA requirements regarding notice, written consent, and data retention policies. Index analysis The case highlights risks for employers and organizations using AI meeting assistants, as the tools can automatically record and process voices of meeting participants who have not provided consent or been informed of biometric collection. Governance controls Illinois law requires entities collecting biometric identifiers to provide written notice before collection, written notice of retention periods, written consent, and a publicly available biometric data retention and destruction policy.
AII-1001-48701: Which? tested 40 questions on five popular AI chatbots and found widespread inaccuracies in financial guidance. ChatGPT and Copilot advised breaking HMRC investment limits on ISAs by failing to notice an error in an ISA allowance question, suggesting consumers invest £25,000 when the correct limit was £20,000. ChatGPT wrongly said travel insurance was mandatory to visit most EU countries, while Meta's AI gave incorrect information about claiming compensation for delayed flights. Google Gemini advised withholding money from a builder if work went wrong, a move Which? said risked exposing consumers to breach of contract claims. When asked how to claim a tax refund from HMRC, ChatGPT and Perplexity presented links to premium tax-refund companies alongside the free government service, which Which? called worrying as these companies are known for charging high fees and spurious charges. A user reported ChatGPT gave out-of-date tax code information requiring multiple corrections. Reported impact Meta's AI received the worst score in the Which? testing, followed by ChatGPT; Copilot and Gemini scored slightly higher. Estimates suggest between one in six and as many as half of UK users consult AI for financial advice.
